newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram hopes budget can be rescued.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram hopes budget can be rescued.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said on Friday efforts were being made to salvage the 1997/98 (April-March) budget but doubts persisted as the ruling coalition faced imminent defeat in parliament.

"I am still hopeful that all political parties will find some way in which parliament can discharge its responsibility of passing the Finance Bill," Chidambaram told reporters during a break in parliamentary debate over a motion of confidence in Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Deve Gowda was expected to lose the vote of confidence, set for later on Friday, but his United Front coalition was holding talks to find a new leader and avert mid-term elections.
The finance minister said the speaker of the lower house, P.A. Sangma, had called a meeting of leaders of all political parties earlier on Friday to discuss the budget.
"As parliamentarians, it is possible to get together to pass the Finance Bill irrespective of the difficulties which the executive faces," Chidambaram said.
But Congress party leader Priya Ranjan Das Munshi, in his reply to the confidence motion, said: "The budget can wait."
Officials said parliament might be asked to sit in a special session during the third week of April to discuss the budget and take a vote.

"The entire investment climate will be affected," said V. Raghuraman, secretary general of Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry, when asked about the impact if the government fell and the budget died in parliament.
"I hope the budget is passed," Raghuraman told Reuters, adding that he still hoped India's political parties would somehow reach consensus on approving the budget.
Presented by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on February 28, the budget would slash corporate taxes, lower income tax and reduce import tariffs.
Share prices, which rallied after the budget was unveiled and fell back when it appeared under threat, were boosted by renewed expectations that the tax and spending blueprint might clear parliament.

Industry leaders said if the budget was not approved by parliament and the country headed for fresh elections, the economy would lose momentum, and investment plans and the flow of foreign funds would be put on hold.
"If there are elections, it would be a great setback to foreign investors," Tushar Sarda, president and chief executive officer of Daewoo Securities, told Reuters.
"The budget was appreciated by all sections of the society," Deve Gowda said, after moving the confidence motion.
The budget reflected government's commitment to continue with economic reforms, Deve Gowda said. But at the same time it took care not to bypass the poor in the process of development.
With both the Congress and the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party directing their deputies to vote against the confidence vote, the fate of Gowda's coalition seemed sealed.
The coalition controls 178 seats in the 542-member lower house, the Congress 140, and the BJP and its allies hold 193.
Last month, parliament temporarily extended government spending programmes pending passage of the budget.
But some key provisions of the budget would lapse if it was not approved by May 14.
